units.title: Crop seasons: kharif and rabi
units.key_idea: Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon (June–July); rabi crops are sown in winter (October–November).
units.body:
When the same kind of plant is grown on a large area, it is called a crop. Wheat, rice, maize and pulses are crops.

In India, crops are grouped by the season they grow in.

Kharif crops are sown when the monsoon rains begin, around June–July, and harvested around September–October. They need a lot of water. Examples: paddy (rice), maize, soyabean, groundnut and cotton.

Rabi crops are sown in winter, around October–November, and harvested around March–April. They grow well in cool weather with less rain. Examples: wheat, gram, pea, mustard and linseed.

Why does this matter? If a farmer sows paddy in winter, it will not get enough water or warmth and the harvest will be poor. Choosing the right crop for the right season is the first step to a good harvest.

Between seasons, some farmers grow a short crop like moong, or plant pulses that make the soil richer for the next crop.
questions: Kharif crops are sown in which season?
Kharif crops are sown with the start of the rains.
Wheat is sown in winter, so it is a rabi crop.
Paddy needs lots of water and is grown in the monsoon.
Rabi crops are usually harvested around:
Rabi crops sown in winter are ready by spring.
Why should paddy not be sown in winter?
It needs a lot of water and warmth
Paddy needs warm, wet conditions of the monsoon.
The same kind of plant grown on a large area
Many plants of the same kind grown together form a crop.
Gram and pea are sown in:
Choosing the right crop for the season helps because:
The crop gets the water and weather it needs
Each crop grows best in its own season.

units.title: Preparing soil and sowing seeds
units.key_idea: Ploughing loosens soil so roots breathe and grow; healthy seeds are sown at the right depth and spacing.
units.body:
Before sowing, the soil must be prepared. Turning and loosening the soil is called tilling or ploughing. It is done with a plough pulled by bullocks or a tractor.

Why plough?
1. Loose soil lets roots go deep easily.
2. Air reaches the roots, and roots need air to breathe.
3. It brings nutrient-rich soil from below to the top.
4. Earthworms and microbes stay active in loose soil.

After ploughing, big lumps are broken and the field is made level with a leveller. A level field holds water evenly.

Next comes sowing. Good seeds are clean and healthy. A simple test: put seeds in a bucket of water. Damaged seeds become hollow and light, so they float. Healthy seeds sink. Use the ones that sink.

Seeds should be sown at the right depth and with proper gaps between them, so plants do not fight for sunlight, water and nutrients. A seed drill attached to a tractor sows seeds evenly at the right depth and covers them with soil, which also protects them from birds.
questions: Loosening and turning the soil is called:
Ploughing or tilling loosens the soil.
Why do roots need loose soil?
To grow deep and get air
Loose soil lets roots spread and breathe.
In the water test, healthy seeds:
Damaged seeds are hollow and float; good ones sink.
Why should seeds be sown with gaps between them?
So plants don't compete for light, water and nutrients
What does a seed drill do?
Sows seeds evenly at the right depth
A seed drill places seeds evenly and covers them with soil.
Why is a field levelled after ploughing?
A level field holds water evenly.
Ploughing helps earthworms and microbes because:
They stay active in loose, airy soil
Loose soil has air and moisture that these helpers need.
Covering seeds with soil after sowing protects them from:
Birds eat seeds left on the surface.

units.title: Water, manure and weeds
units.key_idea: Crops need the right amount of water, nutrients from manure or fertiliser, and protection from weeds.
units.body:
Plants need water and nutrients to grow, and they need to be protected from weeds.

Irrigation: Supplying water to crops at regular times is irrigation. Sources include wells, tube wells, ponds, canals and rivers. Drip irrigation sends water drop by drop to the roots through pipes. Sprinklers spray water like rain. Both save a lot of water, which is very useful where water is scarce.

Manure and fertiliser: Crops take nutrients from the soil, so we must put them back. Manure is made from rotting cow dung and plant waste in a compost pit. It improves soil texture and helps it hold water. Fertilisers like urea are factory-made and give specific nutrients quickly, but using too much harms the soil and pollutes water.

Weeds: Unwanted plants that grow with the crop are weeds. They steal water, sunlight and nutrients. Removing them is weeding. It can be done by hand with a khurpi, or with weedicides. Safety: wear a cloth over your nose and mouth and wash hands when spraying any chemical.
questions: Supplying water to crops at regular times is called:
Which method saves the most water?
Drip irrigation sends water directly to the roots, drop by drop.
Rotting cow dung and plant waste
Manure is natural and made from decomposed organic waste.
Harm the soil and pollute water
Overuse damages soil and pollutes water sources.
Unwanted plants growing with the crop
Weeds compete with crops for water, light and nutrients.
A khurpi is a small hand tool for weeding.
What should you do when spraying weedicide?
Cover nose and mouth and wash hands after
Chemicals can harm people, so protect yourself.
Manure is better for soil texture than fertiliser because it:
Adds organic matter that holds water
Organic matter improves soil and its water-holding ability.

units.title: What is a force?
units.key_idea: A force is a push or a pull; it can start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn or change the shape of an object.
units.body:
When you open a door, you push or pull it. When you draw water from a well, you pull the rope. Every push or pull is called a force.

Force comes from interaction: at least two objects must act on each other. Your hand and the door, or the rope and the bucket.

What can a force do?
1. Make a still object move: kicking a football.
2. Stop a moving object: catching a ball.
3. Change speed: pushing a cycle to make it go faster.
4. Change direction: hitting a cricket ball with a bat.
5. Change shape: pressing dough to make a roti, or squeezing a sponge.

Forces have size (strength) and direction. If two people push a cart in the same direction, their forces add up and the cart moves easily. If they push from opposite sides with equal force, the cart does not move.

The strength of a force is measured in newtons (N).
questions: Any push or pull on an object is a force.
Pressing dough into a roti shows that force can:
Change the shape of an object
Force can change the shape of objects.
Two people push a cart from opposite sides with equal force. The cart:
Equal and opposite forces cancel each other.
Hitting a cricket ball with a bat mainly changes the ball's:
The bat's force sends the ball in a new direction.
Two people push a cart in the same direction. The total force is:
Forces in the same direction add up.
Pulling a bucket from a well is an example of:
Pulling the rope is a force.
To have a force, we need at least:
Force arises from interaction between objects.

units.title: Contact and non-contact forces
units.key_idea: Contact forces act by touching (muscle, friction); non-contact forces act from a distance (magnetic, gravity).
units.body:
Some forces need touching. Others work from a distance.

Contact forces:
1. Muscular force: the force of our muscles, or of a bullock pulling a plough.
2. Friction: the force that slows things down when two surfaces rub. A cycle stops rolling after some time because of friction between the tyres and the road. Friction also helps us walk without slipping. On a wet, oily floor there is less friction, so we slip.

Non-contact forces:
1. Magnetic force: a magnet pulls iron nails without touching them.
2. Gravity: the Earth pulls everything towards it. A mango falls down, not up, because of gravity. The pull of gravity on an object is its weight.
3. Electrostatic force: rub a plastic comb on dry hair, and it can pick up small bits of paper without touching them.

So, a falling mango, a magnet and a charged comb all show forces acting across a gap. A pushing hand, a rolling tyre and a pulling bullock show forces that need contact.
questions: Why does a rolling cycle slowly stop on its own?
Friction opposes motion and slows it down.
A bullock pulling a plough uses:
Animals use their muscles to pull.
Why do we slip on an oily floor?
Oil reduces friction between feet and floor.
A comb rubbed on dry hair picks up bits of paper because of:
Rubbing charges the comb, which attracts paper.
The pull of gravity on an object is called its:
Weight is the force of gravity on a body.
A magnet pulling a nail from a distance shows:
Magnetic force acts across a gap.
Without friction our feet would slide.

units.title: Pressure
units.key_idea: Pressure = Force ÷ Area; the same force on a smaller area gives more pressure.
units.body:
Why is it easy to cut vegetables with a sharp knife but hard with a blunt one? The answer is pressure.

Pressure is the force acting on a unit area:

Pressure = Force ÷ Area

The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure. A sharp knife's edge is very thin, so your push is focused on a tiny area and it cuts easily. A nail has a pointed tip for the same reason.

The opposite is also useful. Spreading force over a large area gives less pressure:
1. School bags have wide straps so they don't hurt your shoulders.
2. Tractors have wide tyres so they don't sink into soft, wet fields.
3. Camels have wide feet, so they walk easily on sand.

Liquids and gases also press. Water presses on the walls of a tank. Water pressure increases with depth, so the bottom of a dam is built thicker. Air around us presses on us too. This is called atmospheric pressure. We don't feel it because the pressure inside our body balances it.
questions: Pressure is force per unit area.
Why does a sharp knife cut better?
Its thin edge gives high pressure
Smaller area means more pressure for the same force.
Why do tractors have wide tyres?
To reduce pressure so they don't sink in soft soil
A wider area spreads the weight and lowers pressure.
Why do school bags have wide straps?
To spread the weight and lower pressure on shoulders
Wide straps reduce pressure on your shoulders.
The bottom of a dam is made thicker because:
Water is lighter at the bottom
A force of 100 N acts on 2 m². The pressure is:
The air around us pressing on us is called:
The air's weight creates atmospheric pressure.
A small tip gives high pressure to enter wood
A small area concentrates the force.
